title: Ezra 5:1–5
context: Ezra 5:1–5 describes how work on the temple begins again after it had stopped (4:24). The prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesy to the Jews in the name of the God of Israel, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin to build, with the prophets helping them. Their preaching is recorded in the books of Haggai and Zechariah (compare Haggai 1:1–15 and Zechariah 1:1; 4:6–10), both dated to the second year of Darius. Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, comes with Shetharbozenai and asks who authorized the building, and he takes the names of the builders. But the eye of their God is on the elders, and the work continues while the matter goes to Darius. This section of Ezra, from 4:8 to 6:18, is written in Aramaic, the language of Persian government, which suits its official letters. Arminian and Reformed readers share the main reading: God stirs his people through his word, and his watchful care protects the work while human authorities deliberate.

verses.text: Now the prophets, Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem. They prophesied to them in the name of the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesy to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel. Arminian readers see God renewing his people’s courage through his word after the work had stopped, calling them to respond in faith and obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s word as the means by which he stirs his people to act. Both traditions note that the books of Haggai and Zechariah record this preaching (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 1:1), and they read the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak rose up and began to build God’s house which is at Jerusalem; and with them were the prophets of God, helping them.
verses.arminianNotes: Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin to build God’s house, and the prophets are with them, helping them. Arminians see leaders responding to God’s word and the prophets supporting the work, not merely speaking from a distance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God working through both civil and priestly leaders and through his prophets. Both traditions read the verse as a picture of God’s people working together under his word, which is shared ground.

verses.text: At the same time Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, came to them, with Shetharbozenai and their companions, and asked them, “Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this wall?”
verses.arminianNotes: Tattenai, governor beyond the River, comes with Shetharbozenai and asks who authorized them to build the house and finish this wall. Arminian readers see a fresh challenge to the work, which tests whether the people will continue in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as part of God’s providence that will end in royal support. Both traditions note that Tattenai acts as a Persian official asking for authority, and they do not describe him as hostile beyond what the text says.

verses.text: They also asked for the names of the men who were making this building.
verses.arminianNotes: They also ask for the names of the men doing the building. Arminians see the builders exposed to possible danger by having their names recorded, which makes their continued work an act of courage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the request as a normal administrative step that God would use for good. Both traditions read the verse as part of the official inquiry that the following letter records.

verses.text: But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they didn’t make them cease until the matter should come to Darius, and an answer should be returned by letter concerning it.
verses.arminianNotes: The eye of their God is on the elders, and the officials do not stop them while the matter goes to Darius. Arminian readers see God’s watchful care protecting his people as they continue faithfully in the work he called them to do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence governing the officials’ decision. Both traditions read the phrase about the eye of God as a central statement of the passage, expressing God’s care for his people, which is shared ground.
